title: Legs! Legs! Legs! (The Periodic Table)
summary: Josh and Chuck explain the periodic table, jokingly titled "Legs! Legs! Legs!". They cover early attempts to classify elements (Aristotle's four elements, John Dalton's atomic theory and early lists, Döbereiner's triads), Dmitri Mendeleev's 1869 table with gaps that later-discovered elements filled, and how elements are ordered by atomic number into periods (rows) and groups (columns). They explain shells and valence electrons, why groups share reactivity, the s/p/d/f blocks and quantum mechanics, and atomic mass as a weighted average of isotopes. Later they discuss particle accelerators and lab-created elements from the 1930s onward (technetium, einsteinium, tennessine, nihonium, moscovium, oganesson), IUPAC naming rules, the separated f-block, alternative table designs such as spirals and Timothy Stowe's 3D table, and relativistic effects on gold and mercury. The episode closes with a listener mail segment about a Halloween episode (the Hermit's eyes not matching his mouth) and a promotion of tour dates.
topics: Stuff You Should Know chemistry episode

segments.title: Tour announcement and opening
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck announce January tour dates in the Pacific Northwest and Northern California (Seattle, Portland, SketchFest San Francisco) and direct listeners to the website and linktree. They then introduce the periodic table episode.

segments.title: Introduction to the periodic table episode
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the topic and admit they find chemistry difficult. Chuck notes that many explainers on the subject are wrong or unclear, and credits Olivia for research help. They preview a basic introduction to the topic.

segments.title: Early element classification and John Dalton
segments.summary: They cover Aristotle's four elements and the later move toward identifying more building blocks. They describe John Dalton's 1803-1804 atomic theory and early lists of elements, including his 1803 list of five, and how chemists weighed elements. Dalton did not discover elements; he proposed ordering them by atomic weight.

segments.title: Patterns and Mendeleev's table
segments.summary: Dalton's element lists grew over time. Döbereiner noticed groups of similar elements such as lithium, sodium, and potassium. Mendeleev arranged elements in 1869 by similarity and left gaps, and three elements discovered in the next fifteen years filled those gaps.

segments.title: Ordering by atomic number
segments.summary: Mendeleev's table became the model. Elements are arranged by atomic number rather than atomic mass, read left to right and top to bottom, starting with hydrogen at one proton.

segments.title: Structure: periods, groups, and shells
segments.summary: The table has seven numbered periods (rows) and eighteen groups (columns), with the f-block shown separately below. Periods correspond to the number of electron shells, and shells hold 2, 8, 18, and 32 electrons. Helium and neon are used as examples.

segments.title: Valence electrons and element reactivity
segments.summary: Groups correspond to the number of valence electrons in the outermost shell, which drives bonding and reactivity. Elements in the same group behave similarly. Fluorine and potassium are used as examples of highly reactive elements with nearly full or nearly empty outer shells.

segments.title: Reading the table as a map
segments.summary: The hosts explain that the table predicts properties from an element's position, such as reactivity, shininess, and whether it reacts violently with water. Silicon is used as an example of how position gives its neighbors and type. Different colored tables may use different schemes.

segments.title: Blocks, quantum mechanics, and electron orbitals
segments.summary: The s, p, d, and f blocks indicate where the highest-energy outermost electron sits, and quantum mechanics was incorporated in the early twentieth century. Chuck explains that the Bohr planetary model is misleading, that electrons occupy probability regions, and invokes Heisenberg's uncertainty principle.

segments.title: Quantum digression and humor
segments.summary: After the quantum explanation, the hosts joke about baseball and the banter moves to thanks for the explanation.

segments.title: Atomic mass, isotopes, and ions
segments.summary: Atomic mass on tables is a weighted average of protons plus neutrons across natural isotopes; carbon is the example at about 12.01. Chuck explains that changing electron count creates ions, while changing protons creates a new element. Electron gain or loss determines positive or negative ion formation.

segments.title: Particle accelerators and lab-created elements
segments.summary: Ernest Lawrence's particle accelerators let scientists collide atoms to make new elements. The hosts link this research to the nuclear bomb and Einstein's advice to Roosevelt. Lab-made elements began in 1937 with technetium, and einsteinium was found in fallout from nuclear tests. Elements beyond uranium are made in labs.

segments.title: Naming new elements
segments.summary: IUPAC naming rules allow elements to be named after minerals, places, countries, properties, scientists, or mythological concepts. Tennessine, nihonium, and moscovium are examples. Yuri Oganessian's element was named oganesson, and his proposed name stardust honoring David Bowie did not meet the criteria.

segments.title: Gaps, the f-block, and alternative tables
segments.summary: Hydrogen's placement is debated, and the f-block lanthanides and actinides are shown separately because their properties differ. Alternative layouts include a 1949 Life magazine spiral and Timothy Stowe's three-dimensional table. The hosts joke about designing their own table.

segments.title: Relativistic effects on heavy elements
segments.summary: Chuck explains that in heavy elements such as gold and mercury, electrons move at a significant fraction of light speed, causing relativistic effects that help explain gold's color and other properties. He notes time and space are bent inside these atoms and wraps up the topic.

segments.title: Listener mail from Owen about the Hermit
segments.summary: A listener named Owen explains his take on the Hermit card's line that the man's eyes didn't match his mouth, suggesting it relates to disingenuous encouragement, and says he is using the description in a song. The hosts respond and invite listeners to send emails to Stuff Podcasts at iHeartRadio dot com.
